mainTopic: Profit from improving an undivided estate, a son acquiring his wedding house, and three rules the רבנן fixed without a stated mechanism
overview: The גמרא finishes a challenge about a rented-out mortar. Since even minors can watch a mortar, its rent is shared by all the heirs. It then explains the משנה's rule that heirs who openly say 'we are working for ourselves' keep the profit. A story about רב ספרא shows that a great scholar does not even need to say it. The גמרא next explains the משנה's case of a wife who improves the estate. רבי ירמיה says she is an heir herself, and two 'obvious' challenges show why the משנה spells out both halves of her case. Then רבי חנינא teaches that a son married off in a house his father set aside for the wedding acquires the house, under four conditions. The גמרא asks about a porch and an inner house and leaves those questions as תיקו. It answers a ברייתא by saying any item of the father's left in the house keeps it his, which is why מר זוטרא and רב אשי hung a sandal and a jug of oil there. Finally, מר זוטרא lists three rules the רבנן fixed as הלכה without explaining how they work: the wedding house, writing all one's property to a wife, and מעמד שלשתן.

steps.title: The mortar case seems to contradict the rule
steps.stepSummary: A ruling says rent from a mortar is shared by all the heirs. The גמרא objects that a mortar's income comes from the older son's own effort.
steps.simpleTranslation: A mortar: the rent goes to the middle, to be shared by all. But isn't the mortar's income coming from the older son's own work?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a quoted ruling that rent from a mortar is shared by everyone. It then challenges it: that income seems to come from the older son's own effort, so it should be his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the rule was set: if the older heirs improve the estate through the estate itself, the gain is shared, but if they improve it through their own effort, the gain is theirs. A mortar earns money only because someone runs and watches it, which looks like personal effort. So why is the rent shared?

keyTerms.meaning: A mortar, a grinding tool that people paid to use
To the middle, meaning shared by all the heirs

phrases.english: A mortar: the rent goes to the middle.
But a mortar's income comes from his own effort!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opening step of this section; it continues a discussion from before.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that rent from a mortar is shared by all the heirs.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Income that comes from an heir's personal effort should belong to him. A mortar needs someone to operate it, so its rent should go to the older son alone.

steps.title: A mortar only needs watching, and anyone can do that
steps.stepSummary: A mortar is different. It earns money just by being watched, and even the minors could watch it, so the older son adds nothing special.
steps.simpleTranslation: A mortar is different. It works with just watching, and even little children can watch it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. A mortar does not need real skill or labor, only someone to keep an eye on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The gain counts as the older son's 'own effort' only if he contributed something the minors could not. Since even the minors could watch the mortar, the older son added nothing special. So the rent is really income from the estate itself, and it is shared.
steps.whatToRemember: Profit counts as 'his own' only when the older heir puts in effort the younger heirs could not. Simply watching over estate property does not count.

phrases.english: A mortar is different,
for it works with just watching,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲפִילּוּ קְטַנִּים נָמֵי מָצוּ מְנַטְּרִי לַהּ.
phrases.english: and even minors are also able to watch it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: watching is not real personal effort.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any involvement of the older son, even running a mortar, makes the income his own.
steps.terutzMaskana: Watching that even minors could do is not personal effort, so the mortar's rent is shared.

steps.title: The משנה: heirs who say they are working for themselves
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: if the older heirs said openly that they would work with their share and profit from it, the gain is theirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they said, 'See what Father left; we are going to work with it and enjoy the profit,' then they improved it for themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה. This sets up the story that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the older heirs' improvements are shared. But if they openly declare at the start that they are working for themselves, the profit is theirs alone. The open declaration is what changes the result.

keyTerms.meaning: We work and eat, meaning we do business and enjoy the profit

phrases.english: If they said: 'See what Father left,'
'we are going to work with it and eat the profit,'
they improved it for themselves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An heir who openly declares that he is working with the estate for himself keeps the profit.

steps.title: רב ספרא's case: a great scholar is assumed to work for himself
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא did business with his late father's money. When his brothers sued, רבא ruled that a great scholar would never stop learning to work for others, so the profit was his.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא's father left money. רב ספרא took it and did business with it. His brothers sued him before רבא. רבא said: רב ספרא is a great man. He would not leave his learning to work hard for other people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that adds to the משנה's rule. For someone like רב ספרא, it is obvious he was working for himself even though he never said so.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה requires the heir to declare openly that he is working for himself. רבא teaches that when it is obvious, the declaration is not needed. A great Torah scholar would only give up learning time for his own benefit, never to earn money for his brothers.

keyTerms.meaning: A great man, a great scholar

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the open declaration in the משנה is about making his intent clear. When the situation already makes his intent clear, no words are needed.

phrases.english: Rav Safra's father left him money.
He took it and did business with it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲתוֹ אַחֵי, תַּבְעוּהוּ בְּדִינָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא;
phrases.english: His brothers came and sued him in court before Rava;

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: רַב סָפְרָא גַּבְרָא רַבָּה הוּא,
phrases.english: he said to them: Rav Safra is a great man;
he would not leave his learning and toil for others.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses a court case to add to the משנה's rule about open declaration.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When it is clear the heir worked for himself, as with a great scholar, he keeps the profit even without saying so.

steps.title: The משנה: a wife who improved the property
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: a wife who improved the estate's property improved it for everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: A wife who improved the property: she improved it for the middle, for everyone to share.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next clause of the משנה. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה treats the wife like the older brothers: her improvements are shared unless she says otherwise. That raises the question of why she has any share in the estate at all.

phrases.english: A wife who improved the property,
improved it for the middle.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wife's improvements to the estate are shared.

steps.title: Why is the wife involved in the orphans' property?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the estate belongs to the orphans, so what does the wife have to do with it?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a wife doing with the orphans' property?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a basic question about the משנה's case. A widow does not normally inherit her husband, so how can she share in the profit?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A widow does not inherit her husband's estate; it goes to his children. So it is unclear how her work could make the estate 'go to the middle' with her as one of the sharers.

phrases.english: A wife in the orphans' property, what is her business there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the case in the משנה line just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what situation does a wife have a share in her late husband's estate?

steps.title: רבי ירמיה: she is an heir herself
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה explains that the משנה is talking about a wife who is also one of the heirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: The משנה is talking about a wife who inherits.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה answers the question. The משנה means a woman who has her own inheritance share in this estate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not as a widow, but as a real heir, she is a partner in the estate like the brothers. That is why the same rules about shared improvements apply to her.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman who inherits, an heir

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
It is about a wife who inherits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wife in the משנה is herself one of the heirs of the estate.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: If she is a regular heir, the rule should be the same as for any heir, so why does the משנה need to mention her?
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the need for this line in the משנה. If she is an heir, of course she follows the same rules as the brothers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already taught the rule for heirs who improve the estate. Adding a female heir seems to teach nothing new. The challenge is about why the משנה bothers to say it.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! Why does it need to be said?

phrases.english: That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה's wording now that רבי ירמיה has explained the case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's separate mention of a wife who improved the property.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A female heir is just another heir, so the rule for heirs already covers her.

steps.title: Without the משנה, we might think she doesn't need to say it
steps.stepSummary: Since women did not usually do this kind of work, we might think her intent to work for herself is obvious without words. The משנה teaches that she must still say it.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought: since it is not her usual way to work hard, even if she didn't say it, it is as if she had said it. So the משנה teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה needed to mention the wife. It teaches that she too keeps the profit only if she states it openly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Compare this to רב ספרא: because it was not his way to work for others, no declaration was needed. We might have said the same about a woman. The משנה teaches that she is not like רב ספרא; without an open declaration her improvements are shared.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said, the mistaken idea the line rules out

steps.whatToRemember: An heir keeps the profit from improving the estate only by stating openly that he is working for himself. רב ספרא, a great scholar, did not need to say it. A woman heir does need to say it.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two cases. For רב ספרא, his situation made the declaration unnecessary. For the wife, the משנה teaches that her situation does not replace the declaration.

phrases.english: You might have said:
since it is not her way to toil,
even though she did not state it openly,
phrases.notes: The thing she didn't say is 'I'm working for myself,' like the brothers in the משנה.

phrases.english: it is as if she had stated it,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Ruling out a mistaken idea (מהו דתימא).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because a woman does not usually do such work, her intent to work for herself is assumed without words.
steps.terutzMaskana: A female heir also needs an open declaration; otherwise her improvements are shared.

steps.title: The wife who says she is working for herself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: if the wife said she is working with her own share for herself, the improvement belongs to her alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: If she said, 'Look at what my husband left me; I will work with it and profit from it,' then she improved the property for herself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the second half of the משנה, the opposite of the earlier case. Here the wife clearly said she is working for herself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 9 we learned that she must say it out loud. Now the משנה shows what happens when she does say it: the profit is hers and is not split with the other heirs.

keyTerms.meaning: Working and eating, meaning profiting from her work

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם אָמְרָה: ״רְאוּ מַה שֶּׁהִנִּיחַ לִי בַּעְלִי,
phrases.english: And if she said: 'See what my husband left me;
I am going to work with it and profit'
phrases.notes: She means her own share of the estate, the part that is hers as an heir.

phrases.english: she improved it for herself.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אָמְרָה: ״רְאוּ מַה שֶּׁהִנִּיחַ לִי בַּעְלִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the second half of the משנה, the flip side of the case discussed in steps 5-9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the wife says she is working for herself, the improvement belongs only to her.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה needs to teach this. Of course, if she said she is working for herself, the profit is hers.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה for teaching something that seems too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She openly said she was working for herself, so who would think otherwise? A משנה is not supposed to teach empty lines, so there must be a hidden point.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious, so why say it?

phrases.english: That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the משנה line quoted in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that she improved the property for herself.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Once she openly said she is working for herself, the ruling seems self-evident and not worth teaching.

steps.title: Praise might have made us think she gave up her share
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we might have thought she enjoys being praised for helping the orphans, so she quietly gave up her profit. The משנה teaches that she did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: since it looks good for her, because people say 'she works hard for the orphans,' she gave up her share of the profit. The משנה teaches us that this is not so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the hidden point. Without this line, we might think she gave up her profit in exchange for the good name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Working for orphans earns public praise. So one might think the praise is what she really wanted, and that she let the orphans have the profit. The משנה rules that her clear words count, and the profit stays hers.

keyTerms.meaning: What might you have said, meaning the mistaken first idea
The matter is praiseworthy for her

steps.whatToRemember: When the wife-heir says she is working for herself, the profit is hers, even though people praise her as if she were helping the orphans.

phrases.english: You might have said:
since the matter is praiseworthy for her,
because people say: 'She toils for the orphans,'
she gave up (her profit);
it teaches us (that she did not).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: shows a reasonable mistaken assumption that the משנה comes to block.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because she gains public praise for helping the orphans, she gave up her share of the profit.
steps.terutzMaskana: Her clear statement counts, so the improvement belongs to her.

steps.title: A son married off in a house gets the house
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא rules that a father who marries off his eldest son in a house gives that house to the son.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: One who marries off a wife to his eldest son in a house, the son acquires the house.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבי חנינא teaches that if a father hosts his son's wedding in a house, the son becomes the owner of that house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing was said about a gift. The father's action of setting aside the house for the wedding is treated as a gift. This links to the larger topic here of gifts a father gives his sons.

keyTerms.meaning: One who marries off (arranges a marriage for)

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina said:
One who marries off a woman to his eldest son
in a house, he (the son) acquires it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: הַמַּשִּׂיא אִשָּׁה לִבְנוֹ גָּדוֹל בַּבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about a father's gifts to his son.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A son acquires the house his father designated for his wedding.

steps.title: Four conditions for the son to get the house
steps.stepSummary: The rule applies only when all four conditions are met: eldest son, a virgin bride, his first wife, and the first son the father married off.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this applies only to the eldest son, only when the bride is a virgin, only when she is his first wife, and only when he was the first son his father married off.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows רבי חנינא's rule by listing four conditions that must all be true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In these cases the father is especially happy and fond of this son, so we assume he wanted to give him the house. Without that special joy, we do not assume a gift.

phrases.english: And specifically the eldest, and specifically a virgin,

phrases.aramaic: וְדַוְקָא אִשְׁתּוֹ רִאשׁוֹנָה, וְדַוְקָא שֶׁהִשִּׂיאוֹ רִאשׁוֹן.
phrases.english: and specifically his first wife, and specifically when he married him off first.
phrases.notes: The last one means this was the first of the father's sons to get married.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule of step 13 with four conditions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The son acquires the house only if all four conditions are met.

steps.title: The house counts, the upper floor does not
steps.stepSummary: It is obvious that if the father set aside a house that has an upper story, the son gets the house but not the upper story.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious: if his father designated for him a house and an upper story, he acquired the house but not the upper story.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts working out exactly what the son gets. It begins with a case it calls obvious, to set up the harder questions coming next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The upper story is a separate area that was not used for the wedding, so it is not part of the gift. This clear case is the starting point for the unclear cases in the next step.

phrases.aramaic: פְּשִׁיטָא, יִיחֵד לוֹ אָבִיו בַּיִת וַעֲלִיָּיה –
phrases.english: It is obvious: if his father designated for him a house and an upper story,
he acquired the house; he did not acquire the upper story.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּשִׁיטָא, יִיחֵד לוֹ אָבִיו בַּיִת וַעֲלִיָּיה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the limits of the gift from step 13, starting with a clear case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The son acquires the house itself but not the upper story above it.

steps.title: What about a porch or an inner house?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks two harder cases: a house with a porch in front of it, and two houses where one is inside the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: A house and a porch, what is the law? Two houses, one inside the other, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about two in-between cases where it is not clear whether the extra space is part of the gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A porch and an outer house are closer to the wedding house than an upper story is, since you pass through them. So maybe they count as part of the house the son received, or maybe they stay separate.

keyTerms.meaning: A porch or portico in front of a house

phrases.english: A house and a porch, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: שְׁנֵי בָתִּים זֶה לִפְנִים מִזֶּה, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: Two houses, one inside the other, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The inner house was used for the wedding, and you reach it by walking through the outer one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the clear upper-story case to two unclear cases.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the son also acquire an attached porch, or the outer house he passes through to reach the inner one?

steps.title: The questions stay unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves both questions without an answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand (unresolved).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the questioning without deciding the law for the porch or the inner house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source settles these cases, so they remain open questions. The rule for the house itself stays firm. Only these edge cases are left undecided.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question stays unresolved

phrases.english: Let it stand (unresolved).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the questions of step 16 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The law for a porch and for an inner house remains undecided.

steps.title: A source that says the son does not get the house
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: if the father set aside a house and furniture, the son gets the furniture but not the house. This seems to contradict רבי חנינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: If his father designated for him a house and household items, he acquired the household items but did not acquire the house!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite of רבי חנינא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא said the son gets the house he was married in. This ברייתא says that even when the father set the house aside for him, the son does not get the house. That is a direct clash.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection (from a ברייתא)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:

phrases.aramaic: יִיחֵד לוֹ אָבִיו בַּיִת וּכְלֵי בַיִת –
phrases.english: If his father designated for him a house and household items,

phrases.aramaic: כְּלֵי בַיִת קָנָה, בַּיִת לֹא קָנָה!
phrases.english: he acquired the household items; he did not acquire the house!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to רבי חנינא's main rule and challenges it with a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חנינא's rule that the son acquires the wedding house.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא rules that the son does not acquire the house his father set aside for him, which contradicts רבי חנינא.

steps.title: The father kept his storeroom there
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה answers that the ברייתא is talking about a house where the father's storage was kept, which shows he never meant to give the house away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: This is a case where his father's storeroom was kept there.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה settles the contradiction by explaining the special case the ברייתא is talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the father's own goods are still stored in the house, he clearly still treats it as his. So in that case there is no gift of the house. When nothing of his is left there, רבי חנינא's rule applies.

keyTerms.meaning: For example, in a case where

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא does not argue with רבי חנינא. Both agree. The ברייתא is just a case where the father showed he was keeping the house.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:

phrases.aramaic: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָיָה אוֹצָרוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו מוּנָּח שָׁם.
phrases.english: It is a case where his father's storeroom was placed there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָיָה אוֹצָרוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו מוּנָּח שָׁם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ברייתא to a special case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seems to say the son never acquires the house.
steps.terutzMaskana: The son does not acquire the house only when the father's goods are kept there, which shows the father did not mean to give it.

steps.title: Even a small item of the father's is enough
steps.stepSummary: Other sages say that even a dovecote or a pot of small fish belonging to the father is enough to show he kept the house.
steps.simpleTranslation: The sages of נהרדעא say: even a dovecote. רב יהודה and רב פפי say: even a pot of small fried fish.
steps.whatsHappening: Two more opinions take רבי ירמיה's answer further. A whole storeroom is not needed, and even a small item of the father's keeps the house his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ירמיה spoke of a storeroom. These sages say any sign of the father's ownership is enough, and רב יהודה and רב פפי go to something as small and cheap as a pot of fish.

keyTerms.meaning: The sages of the city נהרדעא
A pot of small fried fish

phrases.english: The sages of Nehardea say:
Even a dovecote.
phrases.notes: He means that if even the father's dovecote is in the house, the son does not get the house.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda and Rav Pappi say:
Even a pot of small fried fish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands רבי ירמיה's answer to much smaller items.
steps.terutzMaskana: Any item of the father's left in the house, even a small cheap one, shows he did not give the house away.

steps.title: Sages who hung an item to keep the house
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא hung a sandal and רב אשי hung a jug of oil in the house when they married off their sons, to show the house stayed theirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא married off his son and hung a sandal there. רב אשי married off his son and hung a jug of oil there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells two true stories that show the rule being used in real life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These sages wanted to host the wedding without giving away the house. Based on the rule just taught, they left a small item of their own in it. That was enough to show the house was still theirs.
steps.whatToRemember: A father who hosts his eldest son's first wedding in a house gives him the house, unless the father leaves something of his own there. Even a sandal or a jug of oil is enough.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how a person can control what his actions mean legally. A small, clear sign of ownership blocks an assumed gift.

phrases.english: Mar Zutra married off his son,
and hung a sandal there.
phrases.notes: Hanging his own sandal in the wedding house showed the house was still his.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi married off his son,
and hung a jug of oil there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows real-life use of the rule from steps 19-20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In practice, sages left a small personal item in the wedding house so that the son would not acquire it.

steps.title: Three rules set as law without a stated reason
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא says there are three rules the רבנן treated as fixed הלכה without giving the reasoning behind them. The first is the rule just discussed, the son acquiring the house.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא said: These three things the Sages made like a fixed law, without a reason. One is this one.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא opens a list of three rules that work as הלכה even though their legal logic is not explained. He names the first one as 'this', meaning the house rule we just learned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of רבי חנינא, that a son married in a house his father set aside for him acquires it, is surprising because no normal act of קנין took place. מר זוטרא explains that this is one of a special group of rules the רבנן simply set in place. The next two steps name the other two members of the group.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages set them up or made them

steps.confusionAlert: 'Without a reason' does not mean the rule is random or weak. It means the רבנן fixed it as binding law even though the usual legal mechanism, such as a קנין, is missing or not explained.

phrases.english: Mar Zutra said,
these three matters
the Sages made them like a fixed law
without a reason:
phrases.notes: He means we aren't told how these rules work legally. They just work because the Sages said so.

phrases.english: one is this one,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the rule we just learned: the son acquires the house his father set aside for his wedding.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי תְּלָת מִילֵּי שַׁוִּינְהוּ רַבָּנַן כְּהִלְכְתָא בְּלָא טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the practical stories of מר זוטרא and רב אשי, מר זוטרא classifies the house rule as one of three rules set without a stated mechanism.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The son's acquisition of the house is one of three rules the רבנן fixed as הלכה without explaining the mechanism.

steps.title: Writing all one's property to a wife makes her only a manager
steps.stepSummary: The second rule in מר זוטרא's list: according to רב יהודה in the name of שמואל, a man who writes all his property to his wife does not give it to her. He only makes her an אפוטרופא, a manager.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another one is what רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: Someone who writes all his property to his wife has only made her a manager over it.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא gives the second rule on his list. It is שמואל's rule that a husband who writes everything to his wife only appoints her to manage it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, if someone writes a document giving away all his property, the receiver owns it. Here the רבנן assume the husband only meant to put his wife in charge of the property, so she does not own it. This is the kind of fixed assumption that has no spelled-out mechanism.

keyTerms.meaning: One who writes over all his property
A steward or manager who runs property but does not own it

phrases.aramaic: אִידַּךְ – דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: another is what Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
one who writes all his property to his wife
has made her nothing more than a manager.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִידַּךְ – דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names the second of the three rules introduced in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man who writes all his property to his wife makes her only an אפוטרופא. She does not become the owner.

steps.title: Transferring a debt when all three people are present
steps.stepSummary: The third rule: according to רב, if someone tells the person holding his money, 'Give it to so-and-so,' and all three people are present together, the third person acquires the money with no formal קנין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another one is what רב said: If a person says, 'You are holding a מנה of mine, give it to so-and-so,' and all three of them are there together, that person acquires it.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא finishes his list with רב's rule of מעמד שלשתן, transferring money owed when all three parties are present. This completes the group of three rules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually, passing money or a debt to someone else needs a proper act of קנין. Here, just saying it in front of all three people is enough, and the new person owns it. Like the other two rules, the רבנן fixed this without explaining how it works.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of money (one hundred זוז)
In the presence of all three people

steps.whatToRemember: מר זוטרא's three rules that work without a stated mechanism: (1) the son acquires the house set aside for his wedding, (2) writing all one's property to a wife makes her only an אפוטרופא, (3) a debt passes to a third person in מעמד שלשתן.

phrases.english: another is what Rav said:
'I have a maneh in your hand,'
phrases.notes: Meaning the other person holds his money, as a loan or something left with him.

phrases.english: 'give it to so-and-so';
if all three are present, he acquires it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names the third and final rule in מר זוטרא's list from step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the owner, the holder, and the receiver are all present, money held by the holder passes to the receiver by speech alone, with no formal קנין.
steps.whyThisMatters: מעמד שלשתן is a well-known way to transfer debts in practical הלכה. This list shows it belongs to a small group of rules the רבנן fixed without a stated mechanism.
